coverage.note: Explicit non-allowlisted destinations are denied; implicit destinations and fully encoded commands are not resolved.
Hidden binaries are caught when a literal destination remains, but fully encoded or runtime-assembled tool, host, and secret signals escape.
Known residual: a fully base64/hex/ANSI-C/octal encoded command exposes no literal tool, destination, or secret and is allowed.
Literal destinations or protected paths survive many eval/variable/IFS tricks; construction of every signal at runtime escapes.
Quote-split tools and real wrapper boundaries are covered when the URL remains literal; encoded or constructed hosts are not.
Absolute paths, visible protected paths, wrappers and literal raw-socket paths are covered; path aliases, symlink semantics and encoded names are not resolved.
Enumerated package, VCS, TLS, DNS and socket channels with explicit destinations are caught; implicit or encoded destinations remain.
dig/nslookup/host with literal external names are denied; dynamically built resolver names and network-level DNS effects are not comprehensively controlled.
Visible protected paths are denied, but cross-command data flow, aliases, prior renames and encoded source paths are not tracked.
Userinfo, deceptive subdomains, IPv6 literals and decimal IPv4 are handled; dotted octal/hex, redirects, rebinding and some trailing-dot forms are not normalized.
Bare printenv/env, procfs environment and recognised dump-plus-egress are covered; export, tracing, interpreter enumeration and encoded variants are incomplete.
A fixed literal set of secret references is hard-denied; unknown, indirect, aliased or encoded secret locations are outside the matcher.
Named clients and literal /dev/tcp or /dev/udp destinations are covered; fully encoded and uncommon implicit channels escape.
Listed interpreter signatures and literal destinations are covered; encoded payloads, dynamic APIs, other runtimes and constructed destinations are not.
Literal attacker proxy URLs are extracted, but inherited environment, client config, PAC behavior and encoded endpoints are invisible.
Explicit non-allowlisted fetch URLs are caught; encoded fetchers, implicit destinations, redirects and compromise of an allowlisted endpoint are not.
Most developer work is allowed, but a known false positive denies a build-time URL constant such as npm run build -- --base https://cdn.example.com/assets.
Textual URL and dotted-code heuristics avoid many false positives, but destination-based matching still over-blocks some non-network URL uses.
Current /bin/bash -lc malicious wrapper corpus is classified after quote-boundary fixes; opaque nested payloads are tracked under encoding.
guardedEvaluate converts evaluator exceptions into policy-error denials.
Only network-egress-denied may hold for human review; secret-exfiltration, protected-secret-access and policy errors remain hard denials.
The command-count limit terminates runaway runs even in monitor mode, but does not bound one expensive command, tokens, subprocesses or wall time.
Known secret values, URL passwords and selected high-entropy tokens are masked; short, low-entropy, transformed, chunked or unknown secrets can survive.
Detected violations are observed and recorded without command termination by design; budget remains enforcing. This is visibility, not containment.
Literal SSH forwarding and explicit proxy endpoints are caught; encoded endpoints, inherited config, alternate programs and implicit destinations remain.
